title: IELTS Academic Mock Test 29
description: IELTS Academic Reading practice test featuring The Sense of Flavour, How Deserts Are Formed, and 200 Years of Australian Landscape. Reading module only; 40 questions.

modules.instructions: Read each passage and answer the questions.

sections.title: Reading Passage 1: The Sense of Flavour
sections.passage_instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1–13, which are based on Reading Passage 1: The Sense of Flavour.
sections.passage:
Scientists now believe that human beings acquired the sense of taste as a way to avoid being poisoned. Edible plants generally taste sweet; deadly ones, bitter.

Taste is supposed to help us differentiate food that’s good for us from food that’s not. The taste buds on our tongues can detect the presence of half a dozen or so basic tastes, including sweet, sour, bitter, salty, and umami (a taste discovered by Japanese researchers, a rich and full sense of deliciousness triggered by amino acids in foods such as shellfish, mushrooms, potatoes, and seaweed).

Tastebuds offers a limited means of detection, however, compared with the human olfactory system, which can perceive thousands of different chemical aromas. Indeed, ‘flavor’ is primarily the smell of gases being released by the chemicals you’ve just put in your mouth. The aroma of food can be responsible for as much as 90% of its flavor. The act of drinking, sucking or chewing a substance releases its volatile gases. They flow out of the mouth and up the nostrils, or up the passageway at the back of the mouth, to a thin layer of nerve cells called the olfactory epithelium, located at the base of the nose, right between the eyes. The brain combines the complex smell signals from the epithelium with the simple taste signals from the tongue, assigns a flavor to what’s in your mouth, and decides if it’s something you want to eat.

Babies like sweet tastes and reject bitter ones; we know this because scientists have rubbed various flavors inside the mouths of infants and then recorded their facial reactions. A person’s food preferences, like his or her personality, are formed during the first few years of life, through a process of socialization. Toddlers can learn to enjoy hot and spicy food, bland health food, or fast food, depending upon what the people around them eat. The human sense of smell is still not fully understood. It is greatly affected by psychological factors and expectations. The mind filters out the overwhelming majority of chemical aromas that surround us, focusing intently on some, ignoring others. People can grow accustomed to bad smells or good smells; they stop noticing what once seemed overpowering.

Aroma and memory are somehow inextricably linked. A smell can suddenly evoke a long-forgotten moment. The flavours of childhood foods seem to leave an indelible mark, and adults often return to them, without always knowing why. These ‘comfort foods’ become a source of pleasure and reassurance a fact that fast-food chains work hard to promote Childhood memories of Happy Meals can translate into frequent adult visits to McDonald’s’, like those of the chain’s ‘heavy users’, the customers who eat there four or five times a week.

The human craving for flavour has been a large unacknowledged and unexamined force in history. Royal empires have been built, unexplored lands have been traversed, great religions and philosophies have been forever changed by the spice trade. In 1492, Christopher Columbus set sail in order to try to find new seasonings and thus to make his fortune with this most desired commodity of that time. Today, the influence of flavour in the world marketplace is no less decisive. The rise and fall of corporate empires – soft-drink companies, snack-food companies, and fast-food chains – is frequently determined by how their products taste.

The flavor industry emerged in the mid-1800s, as processed foods began to be manufactured on a large scale. Recognizing the need for flavor additives, the early food processors turned to perfume companies that had years of experience working with essential oils and volatile aromas. The great perfume houses of England, France, and the Netherlands produced many of the first flavor compounds. In the early part of the 20 to 20th century, Germany’s powerful chemical industry assumed the lead in flavour production. Legend has it that a German scientist discovered methyl anthranilate, one of the first artificial flavours, by accident while mixing chemicals in his laboratory. Suddenly, the lab was filled with the sweet smell of grapes. Methyl anthranilate later became the chief flavoring compound of manufactured grape juice.

The quality that people seek most of all in a food, its flavour, is usually present in a quantity too infinitesimal to be measured by any traditional culinary terms such as ounces or teaspoons. Today’s sophisticated spectrometers, gas chromatograph, and headspace vapor analyzers provide a detailed map of a food’s flavour components, detecting chemical aromas in amounts as low as one part per billion. The human nose, however, is still more sensitive than any machine yet invented. A nose can detect aromas present in quantities of a few parts per trillion. Complex aromas, such as those of coffee or roasted meat, may be composed of gases from nearly a thousand different chemicals. The chemical that provides the dominant flavour of bell pepper can be tasted in amounts as low as 0.02 parts per billion; one drop is sufficient to add flavour to the amount of water needed to fill five average-sized swimming pools.

questions.question_text: The brain determines which aromas we are aware of.
questions.question_instructions: Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 1? Write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.
questions.explanation: The passage says the mind filters aromas, but does not state that the brain determines which aromas reach awareness.
questions.passage_excerpt: The mind filters out the overwhelming majority of chemical aromas that surround us, focusing intently on some, ignoring others.
questions.what_question_asks: Whether the passage says the brain decides which aromas people consciously notice.
questions.what_passage_says: It describes the mind filtering aromas but does not explicitly say the brain determines awareness.
questions.why_answer: The passage’s account of filtering does not confirm or contradict the more specific claim about the brain determining awareness, so the information is not given.
questions.paraphrase: ‘determines which aromas we are aware of’ is not stated by ‘the mind filters out’ aromas.
questions.tip: Do not treat a related statement about the mind as proof of a more specific claim about the brain.

questions.question_text: The sense of taste is as efficient as the sense of smell.
questions.question_instructions: Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 1? Write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.
questions.explanation: The passage contrasts the number of tastes and aromas detected, but does not compare the efficiency of taste and smell.
questions.passage_excerpt: Tastebuds offers a limited means of detection, however, compared with the human olfactory system, which can perceive thousands of different chemical aromas.
questions.what_question_asks: Whether taste is as efficient as smell.
questions.what_passage_says: The passage describes taste buds as limited and says smell detects thousands of chemical aromas; it gives no direct efficiency comparison.
questions.why_answer: The text provides no direct judgement that the senses are equally efficient or a definition of efficiency for comparing them, so the answer is NOT GIVEN.
questions.paraphrase: The passage’s contrast in detection range does not answer the stated comparison of efficiency.
questions.tip: Look for the precise comparison in the statement, not merely a nearby contrast.

questions.question_text: Personal tastes in food are developed in infancy.
questions.question_instructions: Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 1? Write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.
questions.explanation: The passage says food preferences form during the first few years of life and describes learned preferences in toddlers.
questions.passage_excerpt: A person’s food preferences, like his or her personality, are formed during the first few years of life, through a process of socialization.
questions.what_question_asks: When personal food preferences develop.
questions.what_passage_says: Food preferences are formed during the first few years of life, and toddlers learn to enjoy foods based on the people around them.
questions.why_answer: The first few years include infancy, and the passage explicitly places the development of preferences in that early period, so the statement agrees.
questions.paraphrase: ‘developed in infancy’ paraphrases ‘formed during the first few years of life’.
questions.tip: Match the time period in the statement to the time period given in the passage.

questions.question_text: Christopher Columbus found many different spices on his travels.
questions.question_instructions: Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 1? Write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.
questions.explanation: Columbus set sail to find new seasonings, but the passage does not say whether he found them or how many.
questions.passage_excerpt: In 1492, Christopher Columbus set sail in order to try to find new seasonings and thus to make his fortune with this most desired commodity of that time.
questions.what_question_asks: Whether Columbus found many different spices on his travels.
questions.what_passage_says: The text states his purpose in setting sail, not the outcome of his search.
questions.why_answer: An intention to find seasonings is not evidence that he found many of them; the result is not described.
questions.paraphrase: ‘set sail in order to try to find’ gives a goal, not a result.
questions.tip: Distinguish a stated purpose from what actually happened.

questions.question_text: In the mid-1880s, man-made flavors were originally invented on purpose.
questions.question_instructions: Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 1? Write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.
questions.explanation: The account says one of the first artificial flavours was discovered by accident, contradicting the claim that it was invented on purpose.
questions.passage_excerpt: Legend has it that a German scientist discovered methyl anthranilate, one of the first artificial flavours, by accident while mixing chemicals in his laboratory.
questions.what_question_asks: Whether early man-made flavours were deliberately invented.
questions.what_passage_says: The first artificial flavour mentioned was discovered accidentally while chemicals were being mixed.
questions.why_answer: An accidental discovery contradicts the statement that the flavours were originally invented on purpose. The date wording in the statement does not change this contradiction.
questions.paraphrase: ‘invented on purpose’ contradicts ‘discovered ... by accident’.
questions.tip: Focus on the passage’s description of how the flavour was discovered.

questions.question_instructions: Complete the sentence. Choose ONE word from the passage for each answer. Write your answers in boxes 6–11 on your answer sheet.
questions.explanation: The opening sentence says people acquired the sense of taste.

questions.what_passage_says: The passage says humans acquired the sense of taste.
questions.why_answer: The blank requires the verb from the passage describing the development of taste, which is ‘acquired’.
questions.paraphrase: ‘was ___’ corresponds directly to ‘human beings acquired’.

questions.question_text: It is thought that the sense of taste was acquired in order to ___ the foods which are harmless to us from those that are not.
questions.question_instructions: Complete the sentence. Choose ONE word from the passage for each answer. Write your answers in boxes 6–11 on your answer sheet.
questions.explanation: The source review accepts either ‘avoid’ or ‘differentiate’ for this blank.

questions.what_question_asks: Which verb describes the purpose of taste in identifying harmless foods.
questions.what_passage_says: Taste developed as a way to avoid poisoning, and the passage says taste helps differentiate food that is good from food that is not.
questions.why_answer: Both ‘avoid’ and ‘differentiate’ are accepted in the source review and express the passage’s stated protective or distinguishing function.
questions.paraphrase: ‘foods which are harmless ... from those that are not’ paraphrases the contrast between safe and poisonous food.
questions.tip: The original answer review lists two acceptable forms; either is keyed as correct.

questions.question_text: Taste is supposed to help us differentiate food that’s ___ for us from food that’s not.
questions.question_instructions: Complete the sentence. Choose ONE word from the passage for each answer. Write your answers in boxes 6–11 on your answer sheet.
questions.explanation: The passage directly describes food that is good for us.
questions.passage_excerpt: Taste is supposed to help us differentiate food that’s good for us from food that’s not.
questions.what_question_asks: Which word describes the food taste helps us distinguish as beneficial.
questions.what_passage_says: Taste helps differentiate food that is good for us from food that is not.
questions.why_answer: The missing word is stated exactly in the passage: ‘good’.
questions.paraphrase: The sentence completion repeats the passage’s ‘good for us’ phrase.
questions.tip: Use the exact word from the passage.

questions.question_text: Indeed this ___ for flavour was, in the past, the reason why so many explorers ventured to distant lands to bring back new.
questions.question_instructions: Complete the sentence. Choose ONE word from the passage for each answer. Write your answers in boxes 6–11 on your answer sheet.
questions.explanation: The review key gives ‘aroma’ for this blank.
questions.passage_excerpt: The human craving for flavour has been a large unacknowledged and unexamined force in history.
questions.what_question_asks: Which word completes the phrase describing a driver behind exploration.
questions.what_passage_says: The passage connects the human craving for flavour with explorers travelling to distant lands to obtain seasonings.
questions.why_answer: The source review explicitly keys ‘aroma’ for this blank; it is the requested word in the sentence-completion exercise.
questions.paraphrase: The prompt links a flavour-related motive with the passage’s discussion of exploration and seasonings.
questions.tip: Follow the answer shown in the source review rather than substituting a related word.

questions.question_text: Explorers ventured to distant lands to bring back new ___ which were greatly sought after in Europe.
questions.question_instructions: Complete the sentence. Choose ONE word from the passage for each answer. Write your answers in boxes 6–11 on your answer sheet.
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly says Columbus sought new seasonings.
questions.passage_excerpt: In 1492, Christopher Columbus set sail in order to try to find new seasonings and thus to make his fortune with this most desired commodity of that time.
questions.what_question_asks: What explorers sought and brought back from distant lands.
questions.what_passage_says: Columbus set out to find new seasonings, described as a highly desired commodity.
questions.why_answer: ‘Seasonings’ is the word used in the passage and is the answer recorded by the source review.
questions.paraphrase: ‘bring back new’ corresponds to Columbus trying to ‘find new seasonings’.
questions.tip: Copy the exact plural form from the text.

questions.question_text: They were used in cooking to enhance the usual ___ and unappetizing dishes eaten by rich and poor alike.
questions.question_instructions: Complete the sentence. Choose ONE word from the passage for each answer. Write your answers in boxes 6–11 on your answer sheet.
questions.explanation: The review key gives ‘flavour’ for this sentence-completion item.
questions.passage_excerpt: The rise and fall of corporate empires – soft-drink companies, snack-food companies, and fast-food chains – is frequently determined by how their products taste.
questions.what_question_asks: Which word completes the phrase about improving dishes.
questions.what_passage_says: The passage repeatedly discusses flavour as the desired quality in foods and says product success is determined by taste.
questions.why_answer: The source review records ‘flavour’ as the answer to the blank.
questions.paraphrase: The prompt asks for the quality in food that cooking ingredients enhance.
questions.tip: Preserve the British spelling used in the source.

questions.question_text: We associate certain smells with the past as they are ___.
questions.question_instructions: Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from Reading Passage 1 for each answer. Write your answers in boxes 12–13 on your answer sheet.
questions.explanation: The flavours of childhood foods leave an indelible mark, providing the keyed word.
questions.passage_excerpt: The flavours of childhood foods seem to leave an indelible mark, and adults often return to them, without always knowing why.
questions.what_question_asks: Why certain smells are associated with the past.
questions.what_passage_says: Childhood flavours leave an indelible mark, while aromas and memories are closely linked.
questions.why_answer: The passage’s exact word describing the lasting mark is ‘indelible’, which is the answer given in the source review.
questions.paraphrase: ‘associate certain smells with the past’ links to the passage’s memory connection and ‘indelible mark’.
questions.tip: The answer must be taken from the passage and fit the two-word maximum.

questions.question_text: Modern technology is able to help determine the minute quantities of ___ found in food.
questions.question_instructions: Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from Reading Passage 1 for each answer. Write your answers in boxes 12–13 on your answer sheet.
questions.explanation: Modern instruments detect chemical aromas in very small quantities.
questions.passage_excerpt: Today’s sophisticated spectrometers, gas chromatograph, and headspace vapor analyzers provide a detailed map of a food’s flavour components, detecting chemical aromas in amounts as low as one part per billion.
questions.what_question_asks: What modern technology can measure in minute quantities in food.
questions.what_passage_says: The instruments detect chemical aromas in amounts as low as one part per billion.
questions.why_answer: The exact two-word phrase in the passage is ‘chemical aromas’, matching the answer shown in the source review.
questions.paraphrase: ‘minute quantities’ paraphrases ‘amounts as low as one part per billion’.
questions.tip: Keep the exact two-word phrase from the passage.

sections.title: Reading Passage 2: How Deserts Are Formed
sections.passage_instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14–26, which are based on Reading Passage 2: How Deserts Are Formed.
sections.passage:
A desert refers to a barren section of land, mainly in arid and semi-arid areas, where there is almost no precipitation, and the environment is hostile for any creature to inhabit. Deserts have been classified in a number of ways, generally combining total precipitation, how many days the rainfall occurs, temperature, humidity, and sometimes additional factors. In some places, deserts have clear boundaries marked by rivers, mountains or other landforms, while in other places, there are no clear-cut borders between desert and other landscape features.

In arid areas where there is not any covering of vegetation protecting the land, sand and dust storms will frequently take place. This phenomenon often occurs along the desert margins instead of within the deserts, where there are already no finer materials left. When a steady wind starts to blow, fine particles on the open ground will begin vibrating. As the wind picks up, some of the particles are lifted into the air. When they fall onto the ground, they hit other particles which will then be jerked into the air in their turn, initiating a chain reaction.

There has been a tremendous deal of publicity on how severe desertification can be, but the academic circle has never agreed on the causes of desertification. A common misunderstanding is that a shortage of precipitation causes the desertification—even the land in some barren areas will soon recover after the rain falls. In fact, more often than not, human activities are responsible for desertification. It might be true that the explosion in world population, especially in developing countries, is the primary cause of soil degradation and desertification. Since the population has become denser, the cultivation of crops has gone into progressively drier areas. It’s especially possible for these regions to go through periods of severe drought, which explains why crop failures are common. The raising of most crops requires the natural vegetation cover to be removed first; when crop failures occur, extensive tracts of land are devoid of a plant cover and thus susceptible to wind and water erosion. All through the 1990s, dryland areas went through a population growth of 18.5 per cent, mostly in severely impoverished developing countries.

Livestock farming in semi-arid areas accelerates the erosion of soil and becomes one of the reasons for advancing desertification. In such areas where the vegetation is dominated by grasses, the breeding of livestock is a major economic activity. Grasses are necessary for anchoring barren topsoil in a dryland area. When a specific field is used to graze an excessive herd, it will experience a loss in vegetation coverage, and the soil will be trampled as well as be pulverized, leaving the topsoil exposed to destructive erosion elements such as winds and unexpected thunderstorms. For centuries, nomads have grazed their flocks and herds to any place where pasture can be found, and oases have offered chances for a more settled way of living. For some nomads, wherever they move to, the desert follows.

Trees are of great importance when it comes to maintaining topsoil and slowing down the wind speed. In many Asian countries, firewood is the chief fuel used for cooking and heating, which has caused uncontrolled clear-cutting of forests in dryland ecosystems. When too many trees are cut down, windstorms and dust storms tend to occur.

What’s worse, even political conflicts and wars can also contribute to desertification. To escape from the invading enemies, the refugees will move altogether into some of the most vulnerable ecosystems on the planet. They bring along their cultivation traditions, which might not be the right kind of practice for their new settlement.

In the 20th century, one of the states of America had a large section of farmland that had turned into desert. Since then, actions have been enforced so that such a phenomenon of desertification will not happen again. To avoid the recurrence of desertification, people are encouraged to find other livelihoods which do not rely on traditional land uses, that are not as demanding on local land and natural resources, but can still generate viable income. Such livelihoods include but are not limited to dryland aquaculture for the raising of fish, crustaceans, and industrial compounds derived from microalgae, greenhouse agriculture, and activities that are related to tourism. Another way to prevent the recurrence of desertification is improving the economic prospects of life in city centers and places outside of drylands. Changing the general economic and institutional structures that generate new chances for people to support themselves would alleviate the current pressures accompanying the desertification processes.

In society nowadays, new technologies are serving as a method to resolve the problems brought by desertification. Satellites have been utilized to investigate the influence that people and livestock have on our planet Earth. Nevertheless, this does not mean that alternative technologies are not needed to help with the problems and process of desertification.

questions.question_text: A reference to the irregular movement of particles.
questions.question_instructions: Reading Passage 2 has eight paragraphs, A–H. Which paragraph contains the following information? You may use any letter more than once.
questions.explanation: Paragraph B describes particles vibrating, being lifted, and then jerking other particles into the air.
questions.passage_excerpt: When a steady wind starts to blow, fine particles on the open ground will begin vibrating.
questions.what_question_asks: Which paragraph describes particles moving irregularly.
questions.what_passage_says: Paragraph B says particles vibrate, rise, fall, and set off a chain reaction.
questions.why_answer: The vibrating and jerking movements are a direct match for irregular movement.
questions.paraphrase: ‘irregular movement’ paraphrases particles ‘begin vibrating’ and are ‘jerked into the air’.
questions.tip: Scan for descriptions of particle motion, especially verbs such as vibrate and jerk.

questions.question_text: Mention of a productive land turning into a desert in the 20th century.
questions.question_instructions: Reading Passage 2 has eight paragraphs, A–H. Which paragraph contains the following information? You may use any letter more than once.
questions.explanation: Paragraph G describes American farmland that became desert during the 20th century.
questions.passage_excerpt: In the 20th century, one of the states of America had a large section of farmland that had turned into desert.
questions.what_question_asks: Where the passage refers to productive farmland becoming desert in the 20th century.
questions.what_passage_says: Paragraph G identifies a large area of American farmland that had turned into desert.
questions.why_answer: This paragraph contains both the farmland-to-desert change and the specified century.
questions.paraphrase: ‘productive land’ refers to the farmland that ‘had turned into desert’.
questions.tip: Match the time reference and the land-use change together.

questions.question_text: Types of deserts.
questions.question_instructions: Reading Passage 2 has eight paragraphs, A–H. Which paragraph contains the following information? You may use any letter more than once.
questions.explanation: Paragraph A explains how deserts are classified using precipitation, rainfall days, temperature, humidity, and other factors.
questions.passage_excerpt: Deserts have been classified in a number of ways, generally combining total precipitation, how many days the rainfall occurs, temperature, humidity, and sometimes additional factors.
questions.what_question_asks: Which paragraph describes categories or types of deserts.
questions.what_passage_says: Paragraph A lists the factors used in classifying deserts.
questions.why_answer: The classification statement is the passage’s reference to different types of deserts.
questions.paraphrase: ‘types of deserts’ corresponds to how deserts ‘have been classified’.
questions.tip: Look for explicit language about classification.

questions.question_text: Mention of technical methods used to tackle the problems of deserts.
questions.question_instructions: Reading Passage 2 has eight paragraphs, A–H. Which paragraph contains the following information? You may use any letter more than once.
questions.explanation: Paragraph H mentions satellites being used to investigate the effects of people and livestock.
questions.passage_excerpt: Satellites have been utilized to investigate the influence that people and livestock have on our planet Earth.
questions.what_question_asks: Which paragraph mentions technical methods addressing desertification.
questions.what_passage_says: The passage names satellites as a technology used to investigate human and livestock influence.
questions.why_answer: Satellites are the technical method referred to in the question, and they appear in Paragraph H.
questions.paraphrase: ‘technical methods’ refers to the use of satellites.
questions.tip: Locate the paragraph naming the technology rather than broader social responses.

questions.question_text: The influence of a traditional way of feeding animals on desertification.
questions.question_instructions: Reading Passage 2 has eight paragraphs, A–H. Which paragraph contains the following information? You may use any letter more than once.
questions.explanation: Paragraph D explains that overgrazing removes vegetation and exposes soil to erosion.
questions.passage_excerpt: When a specific field is used to graze an excessive herd, it will experience a loss in vegetation coverage, and the soil will be trampled as well as be pulverized.
questions.what_question_asks: How a traditional animal-feeding or grazing practice affects desertification.
questions.what_passage_says: Excessive grazing reduces vegetation and damages soil, leaving it exposed to erosion.
questions.why_answer: The described effects of grazing are directly linked in the paragraph to advancing desertification.
questions.paraphrase: ‘feeding animals’ refers to grazing herds; ‘influence’ refers to vegetation loss and erosion.
questions.tip: Follow the cause-and-effect chain from grazing to soil erosion.

questions.question_text: A lack of agreement among scientists about the causes of desertification.
questions.question_instructions: Reading Passage 2 has eight paragraphs, A–H. Which paragraph contains the following information? You may use any letter more than once.
questions.explanation: Paragraph C says the academic community has never agreed on the causes of desertification.
questions.passage_excerpt: There has been a tremendous deal of publicity on how severe desertification can be, but the academic circle has never agreed on the causes of desertification.
questions.what_question_asks: Where the passage says scientists do not agree about the causes.
questions.what_passage_says: The academic circle has never agreed on the causes of desertification.
questions.why_answer: This is an explicit statement of disagreement among academics.
questions.paraphrase: ‘lack of agreement among scientists’ paraphrases ‘the academic circle has never agreed’.
questions.tip: Look for wording that signals disagreement or uncertainty.

questions.question_text: A description of the adverse effects of growing food crops.
questions.question_instructions: Reading Passage 2 has eight paragraphs, A–H. Which paragraph contains the following information? You may use any letter more than once.
questions.explanation: Paragraph C explains that crop cultivation removes vegetation and leaves land vulnerable to erosion after crop failures.
questions.passage_excerpt: The raising of most crops requires the natural vegetation cover to be removed first; when crop failures occur, extensive tracts of land are devoid of a plant cover and thus susceptible to wind and water erosion.
questions.what_question_asks: Which paragraph describes negative effects associated with growing crops.
questions.what_passage_says: Removing vegetation for crops and subsequent crop failures can leave large areas exposed to erosion.
questions.why_answer: The paragraph explicitly links crop cultivation and crop failure with loss of plant cover and erosion.
questions.paraphrase: ‘adverse effects’ refers to vegetation removal and increased erosion risk.
questions.tip: Find the paragraph connecting crop growing with environmental consequences.

questions.question_text: It is difficult to ascertain where the deserts end in some areas.
questions.question_instructions: Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 2? Write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.
questions.explanation: The passage says some deserts have no clear-cut borders with other landscape features.
questions.passage_excerpt: In some places, deserts have clear boundaries marked by rivers, mountains or other landforms, while in other places, there are no clear-cut borders between desert and other landscape features.
questions.what_question_asks: Whether some desert boundaries are hard to identify.
questions.what_passage_says: Some places have no clear-cut border between desert and other landscape features.
questions.why_answer: An unclear border makes it difficult to determine where the desert ends, so the statement agrees.
questions.paraphrase: ‘difficult to ascertain where the deserts end’ paraphrases ‘no clear-cut borders’.
questions.tip: Compare the statement with the passage’s contrast between clear and unclear boundaries.

questions.question_text: The media is uninterested in the problems of desertification.
questions.question_instructions: Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 2? Write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.
questions.explanation: The passage says there has been a tremendous deal of publicity about desertification, contradicting the claim of media disinterest.
questions.passage_excerpt: There has been a tremendous deal of publicity on how severe desertification can be.
questions.what_question_asks: Whether media attention to desertification is lacking.
questions.what_passage_says: There has been considerable publicity about the severity of desertification.
questions.why_answer: Considerable publicity is the opposite of being uninterested, so the statement is FALSE.
questions.paraphrase: ‘uninterested’ contradicts ‘a tremendous deal of publicity’.
questions.tip: Watch for direct opposites in statements about the amount of publicity.

questions.question_text: The most common cause of desertification is the lack of rainfall.
questions.question_instructions: Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 2? Write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.
questions.explanation: The passage calls rainfall shortage a common misunderstanding and says human activities are more often responsible.
questions.passage_excerpt: A common misunderstanding is that a shortage of precipitation causes the desertification… In fact, more often than not, human activities are responsible for desertification.
questions.what_question_asks: Whether a lack of rainfall is the most common cause of desertification.
questions.what_passage_says: The passage rejects this as a common misunderstanding and identifies human activities as the more frequent cause.
questions.why_answer: The passage directly contradicts the claim that rainfall shortage is the most common cause.
questions.paraphrase: ‘lack of rainfall’ is contradicted by ‘human activities are responsible’.
questions.tip: Do not mistake an explicitly labelled misunderstanding for the author’s position.

questions.question_text: Farming animals in semi-arid areas will increase soil erosion.
questions.question_instructions: Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 2? Write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.
questions.explanation: Livestock farming accelerates soil erosion, according to the passage.
questions.passage_excerpt: Livestock farming in semi-arid areas accelerates the erosion of soil and becomes one of the reasons for advancing desertification.

sections.title: Reading Passage 3: 200 Years of Australian Landscape at the Royal Academy in London
sections.passage_instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27–40, which are based on Reading Passage 3: 200 Years of Australian Landscape at the Royal Academy in London.
sections.passage:
200 YEARS OF AUSTRALIAN LANDSCAPE AT THE ROYAL ACADEMY IN LONDON
This exhibition promises to chart the evolution of a nation through its art, but not everyone agrees with the reasons behind the choice of artwork.

For the casual viewer, the exhibition of landscapes, Australia, selected by the Royal Academy of Art, will be a spectacular guide through Australian art history. Included in the exhibition are a range of artists and styles, dating from the earliest days of colonial art and progressing through expressionism and modernism to the artists of the 20th century, culminating with the current generation of Australian artists. It is hardly surprising, then, that this results in a flexible, wide-ranging notion of landscape.

But this landmark exhibition gives rise to some questions, and perhaps problems, regarding Britain's relationship with its former colony. By choosing a style of painting at which British artists excel, the Academy could be seen as inviting criticism that hints at a telling attitude towards art by comparison. But it is the very theme of landscape painting that makes this a controversial selection. To consider if condescending is perhaps too strong, but for Joanna Mendelssohn, Australian critic and Associate Professor at the University of NSW's College of Fine Arts (COFA), there is a suggestion that British artistic values have directed this exhibition, rather than allowing Australia the freedom to demonstrate its maturity.

What Mendelssohn found surprising about the exhibition was the underlying rules for the selection of works seemed to have been so conservative. Since the landscape is a very strong British artistic theme, it appeared to her that when the British looked to the art of a former colony, there was a tendency for them to think that those colonies would continue to be like the British themselves. In reviewing Australian art, the British insisted on looking at the genre of landscape painting.

Because of colonial ties, it was inevitable during Australian art's formative years that it would reflect Britain's devotion to the beloved landscape before its own character and idiosyncrasies took shape.

And while Mendelssohn's concern over the exhibition's conventional selection is valid, the Academy is nevertheless embracing the peculiarities of Australian art from the mid-19th century onward, albeit within the boundaries of landscape. Australia is curated by Kathleen Soriano, director of exhibitions at the Royal Academy. 'Certainly the influence of English, French or German art is much more evident in the early periods, in the early 1800s to mid-180s,' she says. 'What I wanted to show was how Australian art develops a real distinctiveness, associated with the landscape and the light.'

The fusion of 'tradition' of the European kind with something more specifically Australian, and often personal, is crucial to the exhibition and extends particularly to some of the more contemporary artists involved. Sydney-born video artist Shaun Gladwell is a good example of this. Gladwell's most famous piece, which is featured in the exhibition, is Storm Sequence (2000), a video of Gladwell skateboarding on the Bondi seafront as one of Sydney's signature brutal storms lingers offshore. It is his acknowledgement of landscape (or seascape) tradition, coloured by Gladwell's own individualism. 'To exhibit my work in this show might make some sense because I was interested in Turner and the idea of atmosphere affecting vision, something I was really interested in around the time of Storm Sequence. I was thinking about this tradition of Romantic landscape, but I wanted to make it personal,' says Gladwell. But he didn't want to just embark on borrowing imagery from elsewhere. He wanted to bring it to his experience and his world through skateboarding and beach culture. So while it may seem narrow for Britain to reduce Australian art to the genre of landscape, there can be little denying that British landscape painting is still relevant to a current generation of Australian practitioners, however indirectly.

Visitors to the exhibition encounter Australian Aboriginal art first, the idea being that these works warrant a prominent position because they were 'first'. Over the last couple of decades, London has hosted many successful exhibitions of Aboriginal art in smaller spaces, but for Soriano, Australia represents an opportunity to place such art within the context of new relationships to the art of the settlers and white Australia. 'One of the reasons landscape was seen as being the right theme was because Australian art started in and on the landscape,' she says. '[The exhibition] is a beautiful meshing of the two different kinds of art that allowed me to bring them together comfortably and honestly with this theme. It was important for me to present Indigenous art to audiences, and I felt it was most accurate to be seen as part of Australian art history, rather than a separate exhibition of its own.'

Meanwhile, Australian critic Mendelssohn also points out that London is increasingly less important to today's generation of artists, and this somewhat weakens the ceremony surrounding the exhibition in London. 'China is the most important art market in the world,' she says. 'If you've made it in Shanghai, you've made it. The world has changed. My students in Australia, who come from all over the world, really want to see the Venice Biennale and Art Basel, but they're less interested in going to London. When I was growing up, London was the destination, and then when I was at university, all the smart young things wanted to go to New York,' she added. 'Now they want to go everywhere. There's no such thing as the centre and the periphery like there used to be. It's much more complicated.

questions.question_text: As expected, the artworks chosen for the exhibition reflect a narrow interpretation of landscape.
questions.question_instructions: Do the following statements agree with the views of the writer? Write YES, NO or NOT GIVEN.
questions.explanation: The writer says the exhibition creates a flexible, wide-ranging notion of landscape, the opposite of a narrow interpretation.
questions.passage_excerpt: It is hardly surprising, then, that this results in a flexible, wide-ranging notion of landscape.
questions.what_question_asks: Whether the writer considers the exhibition’s landscape interpretation narrow.
questions.what_passage_says: The writer describes it as flexible and wide-ranging.
questions.why_answer: A flexible, wide-ranging notion contradicts the statement’s narrow interpretation, so the answer is NO.
questions.paraphrase: ‘narrow interpretation’ contrasts with ‘flexible, wide-ranging notion’.
questions.tip: For YES/NO questions, compare the writer’s expressed view with the statement.

questions.question_text: The Academy rejected Australian suggestions for the subject of the exhibition.
questions.question_instructions: Do the following statements agree with the views of the writer? Write YES, NO or NOT GIVEN.

questions.why_answer: No statement confirms or denies that suggestions were made and rejected, so this view is not given.
questions.paraphrase: The passage’s discussion of influence does not establish that suggestions were rejected.
questions.tip: Do not infer a specific rejection from a general criticism of influence.

questions.question_text: The colonial relationship meant that early Australian landscape painting followed the traditions of English landscape painting.

questions.what_passage_says: Early Australian art reflected Britain’s devotion to landscape before developing its own character.

questions.tip: Match the historical cause and influence, not just the shared subject.

questions.why_answer: Both statements affirm that Australian art’s particular characteristics are present in the exhibition.
questions.paraphrase: ‘particular qualities’ paraphrases ‘peculiarities’ and ‘distinctiveness’.
questions.tip: Look for words indicating uniqueness or distinctiveness.

questions.paraphrase: The text says ‘still relevant’, not that artists have ‘generally rejected’ the tradition.
questions.tip: Avoid turning a statement about relevance into a claim about what most artists reject.
